text: Uncle Oscar gave five thousand pounds of Pauls winnings to the family lawyer, who was to pay the mother a thousand pounds on each of her next five birthdays. <break time="0.8s" /> The mother, meanwhile, had secretly been drawing furs and dresses for newspaper advertisements, but she earned only several hundred pounds a year, which left her dissatisfied again. <break time="0.8s" /> When the lawyers letter arrived on her birthday, Paul watched her face as she read it, and he saw it harden and grow expressionless, with a cold, determined look about her mouth. <break time="0.8s" /> When he asked whether she had received anything nice for her birthday, she replied in a hard, absent voice, Quite moderately nice, and went off to town to see the lawyer. <break time="0.8s" /> Being in debt, she asked whether the whole five thousand could be advanced at once, and Paul said, Oh, let her have it, then, We can get some more with the other. <break time="0.8s" /> There were new furnishings and flowers, and Paul was to go to Eton, yet the voices in the house suddenly went mad, like a chorus of frogs on a spring evening. <break time="0.8s" /> There must be more money, Oh, now, now w, There must be more money, more than ever, More than ever, the voices screamed, and it frightened Paul terribly. <break time="0.8s" /> He failed to know the winners of the Grand National and the Lincoln, and as the Derby drew near, he grew wild eyed and strange, as if something were going to explode in him. <break time="0.8s" /> But Paul refused, crying that he could not possibly go before the Derby, and his mother, uneasy about him, reminded him that their family had been a gambling family.
